note: Named, resettable examples from the same model. Each starts from the default scene or a small fixture, then sets explicit values (path, value). Paths address radars and targets by id. An example reset restores its seed and parameters.

examples.title: Monostatic scaling
examples.question: Why does twice the range reduce received power by a factor of 16?
examples.explain: Both targets have the same RCS and gains. B is at twice the range of A, so R⁴ is 16 times larger and P_r is one sixteenth (−12.04 dB).

examples.title: Equal delay, unequal power
examples.question: How can equal path sums give different path products?
examples.explain: Both targets lie on the same constant-delay ellipse (R_t + R_r = 28.28 km), so their echo delays match. The path products differ (200 km² and 187.5 km²), so B returns about 0.56 dB more power.

examples.title: Bistatic Doppler null
examples.question: How can a moving target have zero bistatic Doppler?
examples.explain: The target moves along the baseline between the sites. One path gets longer at the rate the other gets shorter, so R_t + R_r stays constant and f_D = 0. The monostatic link from S1 still sees Doppler. The target stays inside the segment and outside the 100 m far-field bound for the 60 s scene.

examples.title: Gain contour crossing
examples.question: How does antenna direction change power without a range change?
examples.explain: The radar and the target do not move, so the range is constant. The antenna turns at 0.5°/s from 30° off the target. The two-way gain changes by up to 60 dB as the beam passes; the 30 dB floor holds it outside the main beam.

examples.title: Aspect response
examples.question: How does synthetic orientation-dependent RCS change the margin?
examples.explain: T4 turns at 3°/s. With the synthetic aspect response, the RCS changes with the body-frame direction to R3, so the margin changes although R3 tracks the target. This is a synthetic sensitivity model, not an electromagnetic scattering solution.

examples.title: Integration
examples.question: How do coherent and noncoherent integration differ?
examples.explain: Coherent integration sums 64 complex samples after phase compensation: N identical aligned pulses give N times the SNR. Noncoherent integration sums squared magnitudes: it needs more single-pulse SNR for the same Pd and Pfa.

examples.title: Direct-path interference
examples.question: How do cancellation and filter sidelobes change the received map?
examples.explain: R2 receives R1's pulse along the 40 km baseline. With 30 dB cancellation the residual direct path and its range sidelobes cover part of the range-Doppler map. Increase the cancellation to see the map clear. The cancellation factor is an assumption, not a simulated adaptive canceller.

examples.title: Coherence errors
examples.question: How do phase and delay errors change the complex sum?
examples.explain: Three receivers use R1's waveform for T3. A 90° residual phase on R2 reduces the coherent sum. Equal weights and independent receiver noise give the denominator w^H C_n w = 3.

examples.title: Frequency convention: constant gain
examples.question: What changes when gain stays fixed, versus physical aperture stays fixed?
examples.explain: Gain is fixed at 30 dBi. P_r scales with λ², so 4 GHz gives (10/4)² = 6.25 times (7.96 dB) more power than 10 GHz for the same RCS.

examples.title: Frequency convention: constant aperture
examples.question: What changes when gain stays fixed, versus physical aperture stays fixed?
examples.explain: Effective aperture is fixed at the value that gives 30 dBi at 10 GHz. G = 4π A_eff/λ², so each gain falls by 7.96 dB at 4 GHz. G_t G_r λ² then scales as 1/λ²: P_r is 7.96 dB lower than at 10 GHz. The beamwidth input stays fixed in this synthetic pattern.
